o:
Fire spreads one ring per minute from all initial fire cells (walls block it). We may wait `t` minutes at the start, then move one cell per minute; we safely escape if we reach the bottom-right before (or exactly when) fire arrives there — arriving at the safehouse at the same minute fire does still counts.

The feasibility of waiting `t` minutes is monotone: if you can escape after waiting `t`, you can escape after waiting any `t' < t`. That monotonicity invites binary search on `t`, with each check done by two BFS passes: one multi-source BFS precomputes fire arrival times, one BFS tests whether a waiting person can thread through cells strictly before fire (with equality allowed only at the safehouse).

Example 3: fire never escapes its walled pocket, so any wait works → 10⁹. Example 2: even with zero wait fire blocks every route → -1.
k: Feasibility is monotone in the wait time, so binary search the answer.
Precompute fire arrival times with one multi-source BFS; a person may enter a grass cell only strictly earlier than fire, except the safehouse where ties are OK.
Unreachable fire cells act as arrival time infinity; if even t = m·n works, the answer is 10⁹.

a.n: Approach 1: Multi-source Fire BFS + Binary Search on Wait Time
a.i: Compute `fire[i][j]` = minute fire first reaches each cell (INF if never). A check(t) runs a person BFS from (0,0) starting at minute t, expanding only into cells reached strictly later than fire (safehouse allows ≤). Binary search the largest feasible t.
s: Multi-source BFS from all fire cells to fill the fire-time grid.
Define check(t): BFS the person; prune cells where arrival ≥ fire time (except target allows equality).
If check(0) fails return -1; binary search max t in [0, m·n]; if the upper bound is feasible return 10⁹.
a.t: O(m·n·log(m·n)) — each binary-search check is a BFS over the grid, and there are log(m·n) ≈ 19 checks.
a.sp: O(m·n) for the fire-time grid, visited marks, and queues.

w: Binary search + double BFS is the cleanest provably-correct solution; some accepted solutions compare fire vs. person arrival times at the safehouse directly, but that misses bottlenecks at intermediate cells. Pitfalls: forgetting the tie-is-safe rule at the safehouse, blocking the start cell when fire reaches it at minute 0, and forgetting the 10⁹ cap when fire is fully contained. Follow-up: solve without binary search by running person and fire BFS simultaneously and tracking slack.
